about: Patient Box v2's example cases (v2.1 added the bridge-and-post and the trauma cases, and the buccal-decay case; v2.2 the proximal root caries, root tips, resorption, sealants-and-temporaries and cracked-tooth cases; v2.3 the implant states, implant bridge and anterior implant cases; v2.4 the two partial dentures, the complete overdenture, the cantilever bridges and the resin-bonded and provisional bridges): made-up patients assembled from modules, checked by node tools/ci/cases.js like a hub's (every module, view and check runs on them) and drawn for the screenshots in its PR. Not on any page. A new hub copies one into its content/core.json's pcases (vault/how-to/draw-a-patient-box-case.md).

questions.stem: From his chart, film and odontogram, how is this patient's periodontitis staged and graded?
why: Stage 3: the 3 mm vertical defect on #30's mesial raises it; Grade C: he smokes 12 cigarettes a day; generalized: 13 of 27 teeth.

questions.stem: What does #14's film show between its roots?
#29 is the front abutment of a three-unit bridge. On the film, what holds the core under its crown?
choices: No post: a core buildup alone
why: Right: a tapered post as bright as the crown's metal runs from the core down the canal, one piece with the core, inside a root canal filling that ends about 1 mm short of the apex. That is a cast post and core. (The bone at #29 is down about 30% of the root: the periodontal side of the case.)
A fiber post is only a little more radiopaque than dentin, so it shows as a faint gray band in the canal, not a post as bright as metal.
A core buildup alone stays in the chamber and the coronal dentin; here something radiopaque reaches well into the root.
A separated instrument is a short, thin bright line in the apical third of a canal, not a wide post that starts at the core.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old fell off her bike yesterday. What does #9's film show?
why: Right: a thin dark line crosses #9's root at about its middle, with the root intact on either side of it. Her gums and bone are in health, so the injury is the whole finding.
A vertical root fracture runs along the root's length (often a J-shaped radiolucency beside a treated root) and is rare in an untreated young tooth; this line runs across the root.
The crown fracture into dentin is #8's: its mesioincisal corner is gone. #9's crown is whole.
The dark line across #9's root is a fracture; it is not part of normal anatomy.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old with a dry mouth. On the drawn cheek-side view, what is the soft, yellow-brown lesion on #22's exposed root?
choices: Recurrent caries at a crown margin
why: Right: #22's gum has receded about 3 mm, and the lesion sits on the exposed root between the CEJ and the gum, spreading along the CEJ. Yellow to light brown and soft is how active root caries looks.
Arrested root caries is dark brown to black, hard and shiny, like #21's lesion next to it, not yellow-brown.
A white-spot lesion is chalky white enamel at the crown's cervical third, like #20's; a root has no enamel.
#22 has no crown. The recurrent caries in this view is #18's, the dark band just below its crown's margin.

pbox: An explorer sticks in a soft lesion on #29's distal root surface; #30's mesial root surface is dark, hard and shiny
questions.stem: A 71-year-old treated for periodontitis ten years ago. On the periapical and the bitewing, what are the dark notches on #29's distal and #30's mesial roots, below the enamel and above the bone?
choices: Root caries, active on #29 and arrested on #30
Root caries, arrested on #29 and active on #30
why: Right: both roots are bared to the mouth where the interdental bone and the papilla are gone, and each has a saucer-shaped radiolucency cut into the root between the CEJ and the crest, its inner edge ill defined. A film can't tell active from arrested; the exam does: #29's is soft (active), #30's dark, hard and shiny (arrested).

Cervical burnout is a dark band at the neck between the enamel's edge and the bone crest with the root's outline intact, and it changes with the film's angle. These lesions cut into the root's outline and look the same on both films.
The exam says the opposite: soft is active, and #30's surface is hard and shiny, which is arrested.
#30's amalgam is DO: its box is on the distal, toward #31. #30's lesion is on its mesial root, nowhere near a restoration's margin.

questions.stem: She would like an implant at #14. On the periapical, what lies in the bone at #14's site?
choices: A root tip left after the extraction
A retained root with its crown decayed away
why: Right: a piece of root about 4 mm long sits where #14's mesiobuccal root was, under the healed ridge. It has a canal down its middle, and a dark PDL space and a bright lamina dura around it, which bone doesn't have. The implant has to be planned around it, or it comes out first.
A dense bone island (idiopathic osteosclerosis) is a radiopaque area with no canal, no PDL space and no lamina dura, blending into the bone around it.

That is #12: its crown is broken off about a millimeter above the CEJ, its top ragged and dark with decay, its root still in its socket. #14's site has no crown or stump; the ridge over it has healed.
A supernumerary tooth has a crown with enamel; this fragment is root only, broken across its coronal end.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old. #8 was knocked out when she was 12 and put back the same day. On the periapical, what is happening along the middle of #8's root?
why: Right: along the middle third of #8's root, on both sides, the PDL space and the lamina dura are gone and the bone runs straight into the root, replacing it. The tooth gives a high, metallic sound on percussion. It is the usual outcome of a replanted tooth whose PDL died while it was out of its socket.
Internal resorption is #9's: a smooth, oval widening of the canal itself, centered on it, the canal's outline lost in it.
External cervical resorption is #7's: an irregular, mottled radiolucency at the neck below the CEJ with the canal's outline still seen through it, and a pink spot through the crown.
External apical resorption is #10's (common after braces): the root shorter than it should be, its end blunted. #8's root keeps its length.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old back for his permanent restorations. On the bitewing, what fills #19's access cavity?
choices: A temporary filling over a cotton pellet
An amalgam over an amalgam core
why: Right: #19 is root filled, and its access is sealed with a bright filling with small dark voids, the look of a hand-packed temporary (the odontogram marks it as one), over a dark cotton pellet in the chamber. The canals are filled; the tooth waits for its permanent restoration.
An amalgam is brighter and dense, with no voids, and there would be no radiolucent pellet under it.
There is no post: the canals hold gutta-percha almost to the apex, and the chamber holds a radiolucent pellet, not resin.
The provisional crown is #20's: a crown-shaped shell, darker than the tooth's own dentin, over its preparation, with a bright cement line under it.

questions.stem: On the odontogram and the drawn view, what is on #18's occlusal surface and in its buccal pit?
why: Right: the odontogram fills #18's O and B in the sealant's color, and the view shows the opaque white sealant in its buccal pit. No film shows a sealant: it is thin, and no more radiopaque than enamel.
A composite is charted in its own color (blue here), and a film would show it bright in the tooth; #18 shows nothing on the films.
The temporary fillings are #19's and #21's: sand-colored with two dots on the odontogram, and bright with voids on the films.
A white-spot lesion is chalky, demineralized enamel, charted as caries. A sealant can go over one (the ADA and AAPD guideline), but nothing here is charted as caries.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old: it hurts when she chews on this side, a sharp zing when she lets go. What is the most likely cause?
why: Right: biting on #19's distolingual cusp hurts, most on release, and transillumination stops at a line across its crown: a cracked tooth. The film looks normal, as it usually does with a crack, and #19 isn't tender to percussion.
Apical periodontitis makes a tooth tender to percussion and shows a widened PDL or a lesion at the apex. #19's percussion is normal, and its apices look normal on the film.
#19's MOD amalgam shows no radiolucency at its margins on the film, and decay doesn't cause a sharp pain on release.
#18's bite test is negative.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old: the gum around her back implant bleeds when she brushes. From the chart, the film and the box, what is #30's diagnosis?
why: Right: #30 bleeds at every site and suppurates at its mesial sites, its pockets reach 6 to 7 mm at the line angles, and its bone is 5 mm below the platform where the film at the crown's delivery had it at 1.5: 3.5 mm lost, past the initial remodeling (under 2 mm). Bleeding or suppuration with bone loss beyond remodeling is peri-implantitis (the 2017 World Workshop).
Mucositis bleeds without bone loss beyond the initial remodeling. #30 has lost 3.5 mm since its crown went on.
That is #29: no bleeding, 2 to 3 mm probings, and its bone where it was at delivery.
A failed implant is mobile, or has lost more than half its length of bone, or has a radiolucent line all round it. #30 is not mobile and keeps bone along most of its 11.5 mm.

questions.stem: On the film, what most likely started #30's disease?
choices: Excess cement left under the crown's mesial margin
The access channel through the crown
An implant placed too close to #31
why: Right: the bright fleck below #30's mesial margin, outside the abutment, is cement left behind when the crown was cemented. It was found in 81% of the implants with peri-implant disease in Wilson's study (2009), and the lecture puts cement-retained crowns at higher risk.
The access channel is #29's: its crown is screw-retained, so there is no cement, and the column through it is the composite and PTFE tape over the screw. #30's crown is cemented and has no channel.
#30 is more than 4 mm from #31's root, well past the 1.5 mm an implant is kept from a tooth.
The crown's material doesn't cause disease; what was left under it does. Metal-ceramic crowns are common on posterior implants.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old at his checkup. From the films and the odontogram, what replaces #20?
choices: A pontic on a three-unit bridge on implants at #19 and #21
A pontic on a bridge joining #19's implant to #21's natural tooth
Nothing: #20 is missing and not replaced
why: Right: #19 and #21 are implants (threaded metal bodies with no roots or ligament), each carrying a metal-ceramic abutment crown, and #20's pontic hangs between them, joined at both contacts. Two implants carry a three-unit bridge (the lecture: a span flexes with its cube, so not usually four).
#21 is an implant too, with no root or PDL space. An implant is never joined to a tooth: the tooth moves 25 to 100 um in its ligament, the implant 3 to 5 um.
No implant is in #20's site: the bone under the pontic is a healed ridge.
The odontogram draws #20's crown with its root crossed out and a bar joining it to #19 and #21: a pontic.

questions.stem: On the bitewing, why does each of #19's and #21's crowns have a column through its middle, down to the screw?
choices: They are screw-retained: it is the screw's access channel, sealed with composite over PTFE tape
Recurrent caries down the middle of each crown
Cement holding the crowns to the abutments
why: Right: a screw-retained crown is held by the abutment screw, reached through a channel from the occlusal; the channel is sealed with PTFE tape over the screw head and composite above it, both less radiopaque than the crown's metal around them.
Decay doesn't form in a straight column through a crown, and these are implant crowns: below them are threaded implants, not teeth.
There are no roots to hold a post: #19 and #21 are implants.
A cemented crown's cement is a thin line at its margin, and has no channel; these crowns are screwed on.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old: her front implant bleeds when she flosses, and the other one feels loose. From the chart, the film and the box, which is right?
why: Right: #8 bleeds at every site with 4 to 5 mm probings, but its bone is where it was when the crown went on (1.5 mm below the platform): inflammation without bone loss, mucositis, reversible. #10 is mobile (2) with a radiolucent line all round it: it has lost its osseointegration, a failed implant.
#8 has lost no bone since delivery, which peri-implantitis needs, and #10's mobility is more than inflammation: a mobile implant has failed.
Neither has bone loss past the initial remodeling; #10 has failed for another reason: it is held in fibrous tissue, not bone.
#8 bleeds at every site, which health never does, and #10's bone is at the crest; its problem is the line round it and its mobility.

questions.stem: What should happen to #10's implant?
choices: Remove it: a mobile implant has failed
Clean and decontaminate its surface without surgery
why: Right: an implant that moves has lost its osseointegration and is held in fibrous tissue (the radiolucent line on the film); it can't be saved and is removed, and the site can be grafted for another later.
Nonsurgical therapy treats mucositis, as on #8, and is the start for peri-implantitis; it can't bring back bone contact once the implant moves.
Never join an implant to a tooth: the tooth moves 25 to 100 um in its ligament, the implant 3 to 5 um, so the joined tooth intrudes and the joint fails.
The crown isn't loose on its abutment; the whole implant moves in the bone.

questions.stem: What is this lower arch's Kennedy classification?
why: Right: both sides end in a free-end space, with no tooth behind it (#18 to #20 on the left, #30 and #31 on the right), which makes Class I. The space at #26 is one more space, so modification 1. #17 and #32, third molars missing and not replaced, aren't counted (Applegate's rules).
Class II has a free end on one side only; here both sides end with no tooth behind the space.
Class III spaces have a tooth standing behind them, and the free ends here have none: #17 to #20 and #30 to #32 are all missing.
Class IV is a single space across the midline in front of every tooth left, and it never has modifications; the free-end spaces here decide the class.

questions.stem: Why do #21 and #29 carry RPI clasps (a mesial rest, a distal proximal plate and an I-bar)?
choices: Every clasp on a partial denture is an RPI
So the rest can go distal, next to the saddle
They stand next to free-end bases: as a base sinks into the ridge, the plate and I-bar move off the tooth instead of levering it
#21 and #29 are loose, and an RPI splints them
why: An RPI is for the abutment next to a distal extension; a tooth with a space bounded on both sides takes a circumferential clasp, which nothing rotates around.
The rest goes mesial on a free-end abutment: a distal rest puts the turning point behind the tooth, so the base sinking pulls the tooth back and lifts the clasp tip into it.

Right: the ridge's mucosa gives far more under a bite than a tooth's ligament, so a free-end base sinks and the denture turns around its rests. With the rest mesial, the proximal plate and the I-bar (at the buccal's height of contour) move down and forward, away from the tooth, instead of torquing it (Kratochvil 1963; Krol 1973).
Neither tooth is mobile, and a clasp isn't a splint: a tooth with mobility 2 or more doesn't carry a clasp at all.

questions.stem: Her major connector is a lingual bar. What lets it be a bar, not a lingual plate?
choices: 9 mm from the lingual gingival margins to the floor of the mouth
A lingual plate is only used in the upper arch
A Class I denture always takes a bar
why: That is a reason for a lingual plate, which rests on the incisors' cingula; her incisors aren't mobile.

Right: a bar needs 8 mm. Its upper border stays 4 mm below the gingival margins and the bar itself is about 4 mm tall, so with less room than that (measured with the tongue raised) the connector becomes a lingual plate (McCracken's).
A lingual plate is a lower connector; the upper ones are a palatal strap, an anterior-posterior strap, a horseshoe or a complete palate.
The class doesn't choose the lower connector: the room to the floor of the mouth, tori, a high frenum and incisors that need support do.

questions.stem: What is this upper arch's Kennedy classification?
why: Class I needs a free end on both sides; on the left, #14 and #15 still stand behind the space at #12.
Class III spaces have a tooth behind them; nothing stands behind #4 on the right.
#16 is a third molar missing and not replaced, so it isn't counted as a space (Applegate's rules); only #12's space adds a modification.
Right: one side ends free (#1 to #3, behind #4), which makes Class II, and the bounded space at #12 is modification 1.

questions.stem: #6 carries a cingulum rest but no clasp. What is it for?
choices: It's an indirect retainer: it stops the free-end base from lifting off the ridge
It holds the denture in by engaging an undercut on #6
It replaces enamel lost on #6's cingulum
why: Right: when sticky food pulls the free-end base up, the denture would turn around the fulcrum line, through #4's and #15's rests. A rest on the far side of that line, as far forward as there is room, such as a canine's cingulum, stops the turn (McCracken's).
A rest sits on a prepared seat and gives support; retention comes from a clasp arm's tip in an undercut, and #6 has no clasp.
A rest seat is a shallow preparation for the framework, not a restoration.
#6 isn't mobile; a rest doesn't brace a tooth sideways, and a mobile tooth carries no clasp.

questions.stem: From the films, what has been done to #6 and #11?
choices: They are root tips left behind after extractions
Posts and cores waiting for crowns
Root canal treatment, the crowns cut to domes just above the gum, the canals sealed with amalgam
why: A root tip has no root filling and a broken, uneven top below the bone; these are filled, smoothly domed and sealed, 2 to 3 mm above the gingival margin.
A post runs deep in the canal with a core built up high for a crown; here the canal holds gutta-percha to near the apex under a short plug, and the top is a low dome.

Right: they are overdenture abutments. Root-filled, cut to a dome 2 to 3 mm above the margin and sealed with amalgam, they sit under the denture's base (Zarb; Ettinger and Qian 2004). The films are taken with the denture out.
An implant is a threaded cylinder with no canal and no ligament space; these are roots in their sockets.

questions.stem: Why keep these two roots under his denture instead of taking them out?
choices: The denture is clasped to them
They keep the ridge under them and give the denture support and feel
They hold the denture in by suction
A tooth with a root canal filling can't be extracted
why: A complete denture has no clasps; it covers the domes and rests on them.

Right: the bone round a kept root stays: over 5 years, about 0.6 mm of the front ridge's height was lost under overdentures, against 5.2 mm under complete dentures (Crum and Rooney 1978). The roots carry some of the bite, and their ligaments still sense it. They need daily cleaning and fluoride, because the base keeps them wet with plaque (Ettinger and Qian 2004).
A denture's suction comes from its border seal on the ridge and palate; domes add no retention unless they carry attachments.
A root-filled tooth can be extracted like any other; these were kept on purpose.

questions.stem: #7 hangs from #6 alone, but #21 hangs from #20 and #19 joined together. Why the difference?
choices: #19 is loose and is splinted to #20
A premolar pontic takes more load: two splinted abutments share it, with the pontic hung mesially
why: None of these teeth is mobile; the join is for the cantilever, not a splint.
A maxillary lateral incisor, a small tooth with light bites, can hang from the canine alone, as #7 does.
Cantilevers hang mesially, toward the front where bites are lighter; a pontic hung distally sits where the bite is heaviest and levers its abutment most.

Right: a cantilevered pontic levers its abutment, so a premolar's is carried by two splinted abutments and hung off the mesial; a lateral incisor's light load needs only the canine (Shillingburg; Rosenstiel). A canine or a full-size molar isn't replaced this way.

questions.stem: #7's resin-bonded bridge has one wing, on #8. Why not wings on both #6 and #8?
choices: One wing does as well or better: with two, the teeth move apart and one wing comes loose unseen
Zirconia can't be bonded to two teeth at once
#6 is too short to hold a wing
Single wings are only used in the lower arch
why: Right: two abutments move differently under a bite, so one wing tends to debond while the other still holds the pontic, and decay starts under the loose one. Single-retainer bridges stay put at least as well: about 19 in 20 of the all-ceramic ones were still in place after ten years (Kern and Sasse 2011; Kern 2005).
Zirconia bonds well after air abrasion with an MDP primer and resin cement; one wing is chosen for how the teeth move, not the material.
Nothing here says #6 is short; a canine has plenty of lingual enamel.
Single-retainer resin-bonded bridges are used for incisors in both arches.

questions.stem: On the film, why does the #29 to #31 bridge look fainter than the teeth beside it?
choices: It's a provisional bridge, in acrylic resin, which is less radiopaque than dentin
why: Decay would be a dark area under a margin, not a whole bridge drawn faint.
Zirconia is more radiopaque than enamel: it would look whiter than the teeth, not fainter.

Right: a provisional bridge in bis-acryl or acrylic resin is less radiopaque than dentin, so on a film it shows as a faint outline over the preparations. The final metal-ceramic or zirconia bridge will look white (Pekkan 2011).
The teeth beside it look as bright as teeth do; only the bridge is faint.
